Method/Genome assembly and variant calling

Reference-based consensus calling

Map reads to a reference and write a complete consensus sequence for each sample, including indels.

When to use this method

Use when

  • The genome is small enough to compare as complete sequences, as with most viruses.
  • Indels carry signal you want to keep, such as deletions that define lineages.
  • You need a genome sequence per sample to share or submit to public databases.
  • The library is amplicon-based or otherwise sequenced to high, even depth.

Use another method when

  • The genome is large (bacteria, fungi), so complete per-sample sequences are impractical to align and most positions are identical. Use Reference-based SNP calling instead.
  • The sample is a pure isolate and no reference is close enough to map reads reliably, or the reference may be missing regions present in your samples. Use De novo assembly instead.
  • Within-sample diversity is the question, such as mixed infections or minor variants, since a consensus keeps only the majority base.

Operation

Genome assembly and variant calling

Implementations

  • iVar consensus

Needs

Clean reads, Reference genome

Produces

Consensus genomes

How it works

Reads are mapped to a reference, and the consensus base is called wherever depth and allele frequency pass set thresholds. Low-coverage positions are written as N so missing data is not mistaken for a reference match. For segmented viruses, a consensus is generated per segment.

The output is one unaligned sequence per sample. Because sequences can differ in length where indels occur, they need a genome alignment step before tree building.

Used by protocols

Specified by

  • Viral phylogenomic surveillanceStep 2

Alternative methods

  • De novo assemblyAssemble each sample's genome from its reads alone, without a reference.
  • Reference-based SNP callingMap reads to a reference, call SNPs, and combine samples into a core SNP alignment of positions present in every sample.
  • Reference-free SNP callingIdentify SNPs shared across samples directly from split k-mers, without a reference genome.
